inline.s: To know the marks of one’s own mind is to know the marks of one’s own true mind. Does the true mind have marks? The true mind is markless, and that is called emptiness-nature. To know the marks of one’s own mind is to understand that such concepts as “self, person, sentient being, and life-span” fundamentally do not exist, that everything is utterly unobtainable and utterly unattached, and that all dharmas are empty. At the same time one must also know that the true mind has boundless wondrous function, and that deluded thoughts and afflictions are all the wondrous function it produces.

One observes the original marks of one’s own mind by relying on “deluded thoughts’ conditioning by states and the arising of thoughts with them.” Where do deluded thoughts come from? They arise from conditioning by states. Deluded thoughts arise and manifest following outer states — this is the arising of deluded thoughts. According to the arising of deluded thoughts, one observes the original marks of one’s own mind. Deluded thoughts exist because of states; if there were only states and no true mind, deluded thoughts could not arise either. For example, states are the wind, the true mind is the water, and deluded thoughts are the waves. Without water, with only wind, no waves can arise. Deluded thoughts that arise from conditioning by states can arise only because there is a true mind; therefore, according to the arising of deluded thoughts one can observe the original marks of one’s own mind. It is like seeing the waves and thereby seeing the water, and thus “recognizing the dharma-body’s own marks.” Our true mind — the dharma-body — is fundamentally markless, but when a state comes, the true mind, conditioned by the state, gives rise to and manifests deluded thoughts. Through the arising of deluded thoughts one can in turn verify the true mind and recognize the markless own-marks of the dharma-body. With eyeballs alone one cannot see things. Through the self-nature’s wondrous function, the eyeballs are used as a tool to produce sight, and only then can one see things. If this markless dharma-body did not produce sight, one would look and not see. When you are sick and your foot hurts badly — ouch! the pain is killing me! — this too is the true mind’s wondrous function: the markless dharma-body produces the sense of touch through the nervous system as a tool, and only then can one feel the pain. Otherwise, how would you know something is wrong with your foot? Without the true mind one would neither feel the pain nor cry out at it. To recognize the true mind through the arising of deluded thoughts — this is called “view.” The Ganges Great Mudrā speaks of this Great Mudrā view over and over. I too am explaining it over and over here; if you still do not understand, then that will not do. In fact it is not that you cannot understand or do not know, but that doubt remains. This is the Mahāyāna Buddhist “seal of the one true mark”! Everyone, doubt no more.
“Fuse deluded thoughts into the dharma-body’s wondrous function, and become thoroughly familiar with the dharma-body. (This is meditation.)”

The “meditation” we speak of is not sitting there motionless to death. How then does one “concentrate”? One concentrates like this: “Fuse deluded thoughts into the dharma-body’s wondrous function, and become thoroughly familiar with the dharma-body.” Fuse these deluded thoughts and the dharma-body’s wondrous function into one body: the dharma-body’s wondrous function is just deluded thoughts, and deluded thoughts are just the dharma-body’s wondrous function, without duality or distinction. Again take waves and water as the metaphor: not only when the waves subside is it entirely water; even when the waves do not subside it is entirely water. Why did we first speak of the waves subsiding? Because then there is a “stillness” there, which is easy to recognize. After recognizing it, one must still strike down this mark of stillness before one is finished. Beings are accustomed to clinging to marks; the mental path of recognizing marks is well worn, while the mental path of realizing marklessness is still unfamiliar. This requires a process of “turning the unfamiliar into the familiar and the familiar into the unfamiliar”; all the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of Buddhism are such a process. The Great Mudrā is the most direct, pointing straight at “fusing deluded thoughts into the dharma-body’s wondrous function.” If you can accept it directly, that is “one thought transcending the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas,” and you directly “become thoroughly familiar with the dharma-body”; only this is truly the great concentration that is neither entering nor emerging. At that time you no longer fear deluded thoughts; let deluded thoughts arise as they will — all are the dharma-body’s wondrous function. Just pay them no attention, do not abide in states, do not cling, and illuminate thus at every moment and in every place, and in time you will become thoroughly familiar with the dharma-body. You may say: “Eh! Why are you still speaking of a process of cultivation? To illuminate thus is not directly and immediately becoming familiar with the dharma-body.” Right! That is because you have not accepted it directly, and I have no choice but to speak this way. If you truly accept it without doubt, what is there to illuminate? Everyone, in accepting this matter you must be very careful: the true cannot be made false, and the false cannot be made true; “like a person drinking water, knowing for himself whether it is cold or warm” — you yourself know best in your own mind. If you cannot accept it without doubt, then you must still illuminate at every moment within walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Speaking is wondrous function, working is also wondrous function; see everything in this way, and when you are thoroughly familiar with it you will recognize only the dharma-body and not outer states — that is called realizing the great Way, and at that time even illumination is no longer needed.
“On the ceasing of thought, be firm and concentrated; thoughts without continuity, and the view of the dharma-body is not forgotten. (This is action.)”

The first and last sentences of this passage speak of “action.” The action method of the Ganges Great Mudrā never departs from the wondrous luminous true mind; it is the supreme action method. If one understands it from a coarse and shallow level, one is very likely to grasp it wrongly. Let us try to analyze this passage on two levels.

The first level: “On the ceasing of thought, be firm and concentrated.” “On the ceasing of thought” means at the point where a thought is cut off, when deluded thoughts have come to rest. “Be firm and concentrated” means the mind does not waver and peacefully enters concentration. “Thoughts without continuity, and the view of the dharma-body is not forgotten”: thoughts without continuity is not a single thought arising — that is “stopping”; the view of the dharma-body is not forgotten is utter distinctness — that is “insight.” You will surely hear that this explanation speaks of the practice of sitting in meditation and entering concentration, the practice of stopping and insight. We have spoken of the Ganges Great Mudrā a good deal already; you will surely say: “This does not seem to be the action method advocated by the Ganges Great Mudrā — but is this passage not saying exactly that?” In fact that is not the meaning. That is a crude understanding of the literal sense, or rather, the surface meaning of the passage. “To explain the meaning by the words is to wrong the Buddhas of the three times.” Now let us go one level deeper, into the inner meaning, and explain this passage.

The second level: “On the ceasing of thought, be firm and concentrated” — it is not that not a single thought arises is called the ceasing of thought. Because “deluded thoughts and afflictions are all the dharma-body’s original-enlightenment wisdom marks,” if one can turn the light around in a single thought and recognize the dharma-body, then deluded thoughts are no longer deluded thoughts. To recognize the dharma-body and not recognize deluded thoughts is “the ceasing of thought.” “On the ceasing of thought, be firm and concentrated” means that on the basis of the understanding “recognize the dharma-body, not deluded thoughts,” one firmly and solidly recognizes the dharma-body — this is the great concentration that is neither entering nor emerging. “Thoughts without continuity, and the view of the dharma-body is not forgotten”: if one forgets that “deluded thoughts and afflictions are all the dharma-body’s original-enlightenment wisdom marks,” then deluded thoughts are deluded thoughts again — that is, thoughts have continuity and the dharma-body is lost from mind. If one is alert at every moment and in every place, firmly recognizing the dharma-body, then the very thought is no-thought; that is thoughts without continuity, and the view of the dharma-body is not forgotten. The former sentence speaks of “the ceasing of thought” — recognizing the dharma-body, that is, the view school, clarifying the mind and seeing the nature. If one can “be firm and concentrated,” then once and for all one is at ease. If one has not attained firmness, then the latter sentence applies; the latter sentence is the illumining action of guarding closely and continuously.

The Diamond Sutra says: “One should give rise to the mind that abides in nothing.” Here “should” means to respond to affairs, to respond to things, to respond to the ten thousand mechanisms. When people come and guests go, one must still accord with them, and it is hard to avoid raising the mind and stirring thoughts — but this is the self-nature’s wondrous function; so long as one does not abide, does not run after the thoughts, that is enough. At the very moment a thought is arising, one does not see that there is any thought to arise; this is called being firm and concentrated. It is not that not a single thought arises and one sits there dead and unmoving. We make use of deluded thoughts to receive people and handle matters, to deal with daily affairs, but we do not run after deluded thoughts. Our true mind is still unattached and unattending, unmoving and unshaking. “Thoughts without continuity” means not to let deluded thoughts continue without cease, seeking without rest. From Zhang San one thinks of Li Si, from Li Si one thinks of Zhao Wu, from Zhao Wu one thinks of Wang Liu… deluded thoughts flying without cease — that is ruinous. At such a time one must give a keen awakening, pay them no attention, and the deluded thoughts are cut off. Yesterday someone asked me about investigating Chan. He said he liked to investigate Chan and was investigating “Who is it that recites the Buddha-name?” but he could never raise the doubt-sensation. I told him: in investigating Chan one must raise the doubt-sensation; if you cannot raise it, that is bad. Either change methods: when a thought comes, ask where it comes from — not paying attention to the thought, but pursuing its place of arising. When the thought ceases, ask where it goes — not retaining the thought, but watching its place of ceasing. It is like a cat catching a mouse: the cat lies in wait at the mouse hole, and the moment the mouse pokes its head out, the cat pounces. The mouse is a metaphor for deluded thoughts; be alert at every moment like the cat, and the moment a deluded thought pokes its head out, immediately pursue where it comes from. When the deluded thought ceases, watch its place of ceasing. This is the method of investigating Chan, and its aim too is to make “thoughts without continuity.” Applying effort thus for a long time, the continuity of thoughts turns from familiar to unfamiliar, and the non-continuity of thoughts turns from unfamiliar to familiar. When the practice is mature and one meets an occasion and a condition, the mind that observes and the thought observed melt into formlessness in a single instant; with a “huo,” subject and object both perish, faculties and objects drop away, and you realize the great Way.

So-called “the view of the dharma-body is not forgotten” is still doing practice: alert at every moment and in every place, not forgetting the dharma-body. This is the action of “view, meditation, and action,” still at the stage of cultivation. At the moment of suddenly realizing the great Way, the view of the dharma-body too is unobtainable. Long ago there was a monk who was good at expounding the Vimalakīrti Sutra. Chan Master Dongshan asked him: “That which cannot be known by wisdom, cannot be known by consciousness — what phrase would you call it?” He answered: “A phrase praising the dharma-body.” Chan Master Dongshan said: “To call it the dharma-body is already to have praised it.” To call it the dharma-body is already to have praised it; to add the praise “that which cannot be known by wisdom, cannot be known by consciousness” is to put a head on top of a head, a needless redundancy. This is the speech of one who has arrived home. Chan Master Dongshan always taught students to “walk the bird path.” The bird path is a narrow way, a sheep’s-gut trail. A monk asked Dongshan: “The Master ordinarily teaches people to walk the bird path. May I ask what the bird path is?” Chan Master Dongshan answered: “Not meeting a single person.” The great road has a stream of carriages and horses and crowds of people; walking the great road is a metaphor for a thicket of miscellaneous thoughts and a whirl of deluded thoughts. The bird path is a narrow, out-of-the-way trail where no one usually walks; walking the bird path is a metaphor for a mind like still water, with not a single thought arising. The monk asked again: “How does one walk it?” Dongshan said: “You must simply walk on with no self-interest underfoot.” Walking the bird path refers to the journey of the mind; “no self-interest underfoot” means the mind-ground has no self-interest, and when the mind-ground has no self-interest, heaven and earth are broad. Why do deluded thoughts fly about and clinging never let go? All arise from one’s own selfish profit. If the mind-ground has no self-interest, deluded thoughts are utterly unobtainable.

The monk asked again: “Just walking the bird path — is that the original face?” Dongshan countered: “Why is the reverend so upside down?” The monk said: “Where is this student upside down?” Chan Master Dongshan said: “If not upside down, why do you take the servant for the master?” The original face is the master; walking the bird path is a method of cultivation, merely wondrous function, a servant, not the master. To take “walking the bird path” as the original face is to call the servant master — is that not upside down? The monk asked again: “What is the original face?” Chan Master Dongshan said: “Not walking the bird path.” If one speaks of the original face, one need not even walk the bird path. Thus “on the ceasing of thought, be firm and concentrated; thoughts without continuity, and the view of the dharma-body is not forgotten” is only an action method. To speak precisely, this sentence is not ultimate; it is still not the original face, it is still “walking the bird path” and still on the journey. When the practice is mature and with a “huo” the original is opened, the view of the dharma-body too is unobtainable, and one “does not walk the bird path” — and indeed has never walked any bird path at all.

blocks.text: 4. The Essential of Essentials of the Great Mudrā

inline.s: “Mind dwelling on the eyes, eyes dwelling on space: this is the essential of all essentials. (One must consult the Yangdu cultivation method.)”

Mind dwelling on the eyes, eyes dwelling on space.” In our ordinary practice the mind must be alert, and the mind must watch the eyes — what is called “the mind-eye.” In his later years Bai Juyi had a line of verse: “How to cross over the mind-eye? One phrase, Amitābha.” He mentions “the mind-eye.” The eyes look at space, that is, the mind-eye contemplates emptiness. It means to empty everything, to make everything unobtainable. Seeing anything at all, one does not hang it on the mind, which is the same as not having seen it. Though one sees, there is nothing seen — it is not closing the eyes and not seeing; though one hears, there is nothing heard — it is not stopping the ears and not hearing. “It is not that one does not see, not that one does not hear; one is clearly aware of it, without clinging to seeing and hearing.” Practicing thus, one can certainly accomplish the great Way. “This is the essential of all essentials” — this is the essential of all mind-essentials. Cultivation requires secrets, and this is the most important of all secrets. This “essential of essentials” may be understood by reference to what “Yangdu” teaches. Yangdu is a lineage of the esoteric school. Its meaning is that all dharmas are indivisible, and the beings of the five destinies are all pure bodies. The pure body is the dharma-body; the bodies of gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings are all the pure dharma-body. Exactly as Chan Master Yongjia says in the Song of Realizing the Way: “The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is the dharma-body.” This is the speech of one who has arrived home. When esoteric cultivation reaches the unsurpassed division, it joins tracks with the Chan school, and so the Chan school is called the “great esoteric school.”
“Apart from the Great Mudrā of the fourth initiation of the esoteric vehicle, it cannot be called the Great Mudrā.”

This speaks of the esoteric school’s regulations concerning “initiation.” Let us explain briefly the origin of “initiation.” Initiation was a custom of ancient India. When a crown prince ascended the throne, an initiation ceremony was held for him. Water from the four great seas was used, with jewels, perfumes, and rare treasures placed in the seawater. Then, mounting a great elephant, the water was poured over the crown prince’s head along the elephant’s tusk. By this form, blessings were invoked for the king’s peace, health, and long life, and for the nation’s tranquility, prosperity, and the people’s longevity and good harvests. Initiation is a symbol of auspiciousness. Śākyamuni Buddha, ever according with beings, followed this custom and also gave initiations to the multitude. Thus the initiation rite was transmitted within Buddhism, and the esoteric school makes much of initiation. But what is this “fourth initiation” spoken of here? The esoteric school makes much of four kinds of initiation and five places; let us explain below:
The first initiation: the light initiation. Light is emitted to shine upon the crown of the Buddha-son’s head.
The second initiation: the sweet-dew initiation. The Buddha-son is initiated with sweet-dew water.
The third initiation: the seed initiation. A seed mantra is visualized and visualized into the practitioner’s mind.
The fourth initiation: the mudrā-holding initiation. Mudrās are formed with the hands and empowered upon five places of the practitioner’s body.
These five places are the five directions’ Buddhas, and so the fourth initiation is also called “the initiation of the five directions’ Buddhas.”
The first: the center. Vairocana Tathāgata (some sutras say Amitābha Tathāgata). It represents the wisdom of the dharma-realm’s essential nature. On the practitioner’s forehead.
The second: the south. Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata. It represents the wisdom of equality. On the practitioner’s right shoulder.
The third: the north. Amoghasiddhi Tathāgata. It represents the wisdom of accomplished action. On the practitioner’s left shoulder.
The fourth: the east. Akṣobhya Tathāgata (the Immovable Tathāgata). It represents the great perfect mirror wisdom. At the practitioner’s heart.
The fifth: the west. Amitābha Tathāgata (some sutras say Vairocana Tathāgata). It represents the wisdom of wondrous observation. At the practitioner’s throat.

To perform the initiation ceremony of the five directions’ Buddhas, empowering the practitioner at five places — forehead, right shoulder, left shoulder, heart, and throat — is called “the fourth initiation.” The esoteric school rules that only after undergoing the ceremony of the fourth initiation does one count as having received the dharma of the Great Mudrā. Without receiving the fourth initiation, one cannot be considered as having the Great Mudrā. In fact, such human initiation ceremonies are only a form. The true initiation must wait until you realize the bodhisattva stage of equal enlightenment and receive initiation from the Buddhas of the ten directions; that is the true initiation. India is the birthplace of Buddhism; when Indian kings passed on the throne they adopted the form of initiation, and Śākyamuni Buddha also used this form to initiate the multitude. Thus the initiation rite was transmitted within the esoteric school. Today, when the esoteric school transmits the Dharma, it initiates students.
“True dharmatā is the true Great Mudrā. Not cultivating, not adjusting, not scattering — this is its supreme method.”

True” — only the true-suchness Buddha-nature can be called true, and so it is called “true reality.” True reality is markless, markless yet nothing is not its mark. “Dharmatā” means being so of itself. Our Buddha-nature is originally this true, having nothing to do with cultivation; it is originally immeasurably luminous and infinitely wondrous in function. Because it is covered by ignorance, it manifests as an ordinary being (this too is wondrous function). True and not false, dharmatā and spontaneously so, “this is the true Great Mudrā.” The Great Mudrā is the one true dharma-realm, it is our wondrous luminous true mind; this is the true Great Mudrā. The fourth initiation is only a form and is not necessarily the true Great Mudrā; to form a mudrā and cultivate a dharma is also not necessarily the true Great Mudrā. The true Great Mudrā is our true mind; it does not need cultivation, it is fundamentally without adjustment and without scattering. If there were scattering, adjustment would be needed; it is without scattering — what is there to adjust? “Not cultivating, not adjusting, not scattering — this is its supreme method”: this is the supreme vehicle’s method. This method is to recognize the true mind in the present moment; only then does one truly attain the Great Mudrā. To recognize the true mind in the present moment, protect the true mind, and keep the true mind from running after states — this is the supreme method of the esoteric school, and the Chan school is the same. A Chan student asked his master: What is Buddha? The master said: If I tell you, I fear you will not believe it. The disciple said: The Master speaks the truth — how would I dare not believe? The master said: If you believe, you are Buddha. The disciple awakened on the spot: Oh, so that is how it is! After accepting it, the disciple guarded it closely and continuously, and in a few years realized the great Way. The reason he could accomplish the Way is that he could accept it directly and guard it closely and continuously in practice. The supreme method of the esoteric school is the same as the Chan school; it too speaks in this way: right now you know cold, know heat, know pain, know itch… this knowing nature is your true mind, and you need only protect it at every moment. You must know that all states are the dharma-body’s wondrous function, and recognize the true mind through states. The true mind is like a mirror, states are like reflections; recognize only the mirror, not the reflections. Practicing thus is the supreme Great Mudrā, the most perfect dharma-gate, the fastest way to Buddhahood.
“‘Emptiness, bliss, and clarity (clarity is also called wisdom)’ — emptiness is no-thought, and so it is also called ‘bliss, clarity, and no-thought.’”

When we spoke above of “the proofs of the Way,” we spoke of “emptiness, bliss, and clarity,” the three kinds of feeling that arise naturally in the course of practicing the Way. Clarity is not necessarily bright light; it means the mind’s light revealing itself, and so clarity is also called wisdom. To be without deluded thoughts yet utterly distinct, the mind empty as if washed — this is the feeling of “emptiness.” “Emptiness is no-thought, and so it is also called bliss, clarity, and no-thought”: sometimes “emptiness, bliss, and clarity” are also called “bliss, clarity, and no-thought.” Bliss is ease and happiness. This happiness cannot be compared with any worldly happiness. Clarity is the true mind’s wondrous luminosity. When the Buddha-nature’s light shines greatly and prajñā-wisdom is revealed, one is certainly open and aboveboard, free and at ease. No-thought does not mean that there is not a single thought; to have thoughts yet not abide in them, so that in their very substance they are empty, is called “no-thought.”
We spoke a great deal of this earlier when speaking of “the proofs of the Way,” so we will not say more here.

“Not giving rise to a mind of correction, and utterly without scattering, one guards one’s own mind. Thus unattached, unconditioned, and spontaneous, one does not transgress the luminous pure essence of one’s own mind — that is like holding a bright lamp in hand, illuminating and breaking through the darkness. This is well guarding the samaya.”

“Not giving rise to a mind of correction” is the “not cultivating, not adjusting” just spoken of. “And utterly without scattering” is the “not scattering” just spoken of. Not cultivating, not adjusting, not scattering — this is its supreme method. “One guards one’s own mind” means guarding the wondrous luminous true mind by this supreme method. The wondrous luminous true mind is original-enlightenment wisdom: fundamentally markless, fundamentally unattached, fundamentally unmoving. It pervades space and fills the dharma-realm, and is fundamentally without scattering. Whether one ascends to heaven or descends to hell, it is ever constant and unchanging. Therefore, when we do the practice of guarding and when we guard our own mind, we should not raise any mind of antidote, grasping and rejecting, or correction; at every moment and in every place, let everything go, empty, numinous, and unattached, and only then do we accord with the true mind. Only thus can one realize the great Way.

Unattached means without clinging; unconditioned means without seeking conditions; spontaneous means according with circumstances. Everything arises by causes and conditions; do not let the mind move following the arising of conditions. As circumstances are, so am I. When circumstances change, I change with them. Do not add any preconceptions; accord with all causes and conditions. If you insist on having your own way, wanting this and that, or accord only reluctantly, then it will not do. “Thus unattached, unconditioned, and spontaneous, one does not transgress the luminous pure essence of one’s own mind”: to be thus unattached, unconditioned, and spontaneous is not to transgress the luminous pure essence of one’s own mind (that is, the self-nature). To transgress is to violate, to overstep. The self-nature is fundamentally unmoving and unshaking, yet you waver and shift; the self-nature is fundamentally neither coming nor going, yet you come and go without cease; the self-nature is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, yet you are born and die without end. This is to transgress the luminous pure essence of one’s own mind! The self-nature is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, yet you waver and shift, come and go, are born and die — you do not accord! We must at every moment accord with the original nature: unattached, unconditioned, spontaneous, and in every place not transgressing the luminous pure essence of our own mind. If one can do this, “that is like holding a bright lamp in hand, illuminating and breaking through the darkness”: it is like holding a bright lamp in hand, so that the darkness is broken through and all before one is light. Then one does not fear pits and hollows on the road ahead, nor walking at night. If you would not fall into a deep pit, you must break through the darkness. Otherwise, if there is a pit ahead, you will not even know it! Therefore we must not let the mind move when facing states. “When the old man at the frontier lost his horse, how did he know it was not a blessing?” “Good fortune lies upon which misfortune leans; misfortune lurks beneath good fortune.” If you see a fine opportunity to get rich and your mind moves, that opportunity may very well ruin you. Why say so? If you do get rich, kidnappers come and carry you off, extort and blackmail you — has it not become a bad thing! In the Tang dynasty the layman Pang Yun sank his ten thousand strings of family wealth into the Xiang River. He said: “Too much gold disorders the human mind.” When wealth and treasures multiply, the mind is disordered, and one invites envy, so that one cannot be at peace. It is a flood of misfortune — do not want it! If we recognize only the wondrous luminous true mind, do not run after states, and are not deluded by money, beauty, and the like, then the Buddha-nature will appear at every moment and the mind will not be disordered. To be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss likewise requires “one mind undistracted”; if the mind is distracted, one cannot be reborn there.

We must at every moment and in every place be unattached, unconditioned, and spontaneous, not transgressing the pure essence of our own mind’s nature, like holding a bright lamp in hand and breaking through the darkness. If one can do this, “this is well guarding the samaya.” What is samaya? It is equality, vow, and non-transgression. Equality: the Buddha and all sentient beings are equal; the luminous pure essence of one’s own mind is exactly the same, with no difference of high and low. There was originally no sea of suffering; only because beings delusively cling and delusively grasp does a boundless sea of suffering appear illusorily. Vow: one must enable everyone to be liberated from the sea of suffering; one must make great vows to save beings. One must learn from Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha: “So long as hell is not empty, I vow not to become a Buddha”; one must learn from Bodhisattva Samantabhadra: to constantly accord with beings, tumbling through the six paths together with them. Non-transgression we have just explained and will not repeat. We must be alert at every moment and in every place, not deluded by states, and at every moment and in every place remove the stains and obstructions, doing away with our habits of defilement. If one meets with a slight setback and beats the retreat — oh! this is too bitter, my hands hurt, my legs are numb, I will not cultivate, I will not cultivate — and the mind is stifled and miserable, so one thinks it is better to be scattered and careless, to go see a play or chat with friends. Watching and chatting, before one knows it one has fallen into the three evil paths. If one truly would end birth and death, one must make great vows, must not fear hardship, and must strive in practice within walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. A mere two hours, or three or four hours, of sitting is not enough; one must be alert at every moment, not be deluded by states, and protect the pure original nature. This is “well guarding the samaya.”
“If one discriminates and clings, does one merely violate the samaya?”

Conversely, if one still discriminates without cease and clings without letting go, is it merely a “violation of the samaya”? That is not merely violating the samaya; it is the seed of six-path transmigration, the seed of hell. To discriminate and cling is plainly the deluded mind stirring wildly, refusing to let go of one’s own selfish profit. Cultivating thus, how can one accord with the vast, empty great Way? Everyone, take note! Non-discrimination is by no means failing to know good and bad; what we mean is that one must not “discriminate without cease,” must not let thought continue after thought and be unable to brake. When the function is in play, good and evil are distinct and right and wrong are clear; once it has been used, there is no stickiness, no love or hate, no grasping or rejecting, no trace left. If one can be like this — direct perception functioning as inferential knowledge, inferential knowledge functioning as direct perception — this is not discrimination. That this is good and that is bad the mind knows perfectly well, but it does not favor good people and loathe bad people; we hope the bad will turn into good, and the good will go further upward.

Long ago, one man in the monastic community stole, which broke the precept of “not stealing,” and he broke it again and again. The steward wanted to expel him from the community. He wept bitterly, begging and confessing. Because he was not a first offender, the steward would not listen to his confession and insisted on expelling him. But the abbot wanted to keep him and give him another chance to mend. The steward and some upright practitioners said to the abbot: “If you keep him, we will all leave.” The abbot said: “Even if you all leave, I will keep him.” The steward said: “Leave we will, but let the matter be made clear. You keep him and not us — is there not one good man among so many of us, that we are not even equal to one precept-breaking monk?” The abbot said: “It is precisely because every one of you is better than he that I keep him and not you. Wherever you go, you can still continue to cultivate. If he leaves, who will take him in? What result can he have but to fall?” These words moved everyone deeply, and no one left. The precept-breaking monk was moved even more, and from then on single-mindedly learned what is good; not only did he never steal again, he strove in practice, and in time he too attained accomplishment. Therefore non-discrimination is by no means confounding black and white and failing to tell right from wrong. It is unconditioned great loving-kindness, great compassion of one substance, not loving or hating, grasping or rejecting for the sake of one’s own selfish profit. This is direct perception functioning as inferential knowledge, inferential knowledge functioning as direct perception: though direct perception does not discriminate, inferential knowledge still knows good and bad. Our Buddha-nature is sentient, not like wood or stone, and yet it must not discriminate or cling. If one discriminates and clings, one not only violates the samaya but becomes the seed of six-path transmigration, and may even fall into hell. To discriminate and cling brings endless trouble!

“One who forever departs from discrimination and clinging, and gives rise to the mind while abiding in nothing, can then see through to the true meaning of all the teachings of the three baskets, without remainder.”

We have said above that if one does not depart from discrimination and clinging, one not only violates the samaya but brings endless trouble; therefore one must “forever depart from discrimination and clinging.” Even if your family wealth amounts to ten thousand strings, you must not cling to it — can you keep it? You cannot! Because you must die in the end, and after you die you cannot take a single cent with you; you go empty-handed. In the end you must let go, and whether you are willing or not, you must let go. Why not be a little wiser and let go right now, thereby gaining great wisdom and great enjoyment? To say nothing of the time of death — even now, before your eyes, you may not be able to keep it. Śākyamuni Buddha said that wealth is “shared by five households.” It is not your own; it is shared with five households. Which five? Water, fire, thieves, the king, and relatives. Your property can be washed away by great floods, burned up by great fires, seized by thieves, confiscated by the king, fought over by relatives. Which part is your own? Once the five households come to take it, whether you let go or not, you must let go. So let us be a little wiser and discriminate and cling no more. We must “forever depart from discrimination and clinging, and give rise to the mind while abiding in nothing”: at all times and in all places to be without discrimination and clinging is called “forever departing.” The mind not greedy or clinging, the intent not sticky, is called “abiding in nothing.” It is not that the mind is like dead ashes, but that lively wondrous function appears before one — this is called “giving rise to the mind.”

If one is indeed like this, “one can then see through to the true meaning of all the teachings of the three baskets, without remainder.” If we can truly be unattached at all times and in all places, and give rise to the numinous, lively, wondrous true mind, we can thoroughly and clearly see the true meaning of the Buddhadharma and understand it without remainder. If we do dead practice — “a withered tree leaning on a cold cliff, three winters without a breath of warmth” — at most we realize the fruit of arhatship, and that is still within transformation birth-and-death. Why? Because he abides unmoving in a pure land outside the three realms, dead there; this is another kind of birth and death. Ordinary beings have birth-and-death in stages; arhats have transformation birth-and-death. Therefore we must give rise to the unattached mind, give rise to the mind of boundless wondrous function. The Diamond Sutra says: “One should give rise to the mind that abides in nothing.” The Sixth Patriarch awakened right there. In response to Shenxiu’s verse, “The body is a bodhi tree; the mind is a bright mirror stand. At every moment wipe it diligently; let no dust cling,” the Sixth Patriarch made a verse: “Bodhi is fundamentally no tree; the bright mirror is also no stand. Fundamentally there is not a single thing — where could dust cling?” Master Shenxiu clung to existence; the Sixth Patriarch’s verse leaned toward emptiness. You say existence, so I say emptiness — in fact both were one-sided, and so the Fifth Patriarch said, “He has not yet seen the nature either.” Some hold that the Fifth Patriarch said this deliberately, fearing that Shenxiu’s supporters would harm the Sixth Patriarch. In fact it was not said falsely; if it were false, why would the Fifth Patriarch still call the Sixth Patriarch into his room at the third watch and instruct him further? The Fifth Patriarch expounded the Diamond Sutra for the Sixth Patriarch, and when he came to “one should give rise to the mind that abides in nothing,” the Sixth Patriarch was greatly enlightened at the words. Ah, the self-nature is originally lively — it is not a blank void, not dead and unmoving! The Sixth Patriarch said with emotion: “How could I have known that the self-nature is itself pure; how could I have known that the self-nature is itself neither born nor extinguished; how could I have known that the self-nature is itself complete; how could I have known that the self-nature is itself unmoving; how could I have known that the self-nature can produce all dharmas.” The Sixth Patriarch said “how could I have known” five times in a row: he had come alive. Before this, what the Sixth Patriarch Huineng understood was in fact one-sided emptiness, dead. “Fundamentally there is not a single thing — where could dust cling?” — empty to the extreme, and this too is not ultimate. The Fifth Patriarch saw that he was good material, and so struck the pestle three times with his staff and left, hinting that he should come to the room at the third watch; he expounded the Diamond Sutra for him and brought him to sudden understanding.

Therefore we must not do dead practice but living practice, giving rise to wondrous function at every moment. “The channel is now just me” — all are my shadows, all are my wondrous function. But “I now am not the channel”; one must not cling to the wondrous function either. We do not fear sentient beings or demons; these too are wondrous function, not a blank nothingness. Some say the Diamond Sutra teaches emptiness, a blank nothingness — that is a mistaken understanding, wrong! The Diamond Sutra teaches boundless wondrous function; it manifests the true mind. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss does exist; there is such a beautiful world: the ground of gold, the seven-jeweled lotus ponds, the water of eight meritorious qualities, the sound of wind and the speech of birds proclaiming the Dharma-sound. It is just that good — of course it truly exists; how could it not? But this is wondrous existence, not substantial existence: it was originally not there, and it is transformed by the vow-power of Amitābha Buddha and the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pool Assembly. Stubborn emptiness is wrong, and substantial existence is wrong too. True emptiness and wondrous existence: empty yet not empty, existent yet not existent; not empty yet empty, not existent yet existent. If one can be like this, one “forever departs from discrimination and clinging,” one “gives rise to the mind while abiding in nothing,” and “can then see through to the true meaning of all the teachings of the three baskets, without remainder.” The Buddhadharma of the three baskets and twelve divisions, the boundless ocean of teachings, can all be understood in the mind. Not one of the three baskets and twelve divisions fails to depict the true mind; once you comprehend the true mind, you have grasped the true meaning. You are then one of the household, no longer an outsider; the things in your own house you of course see through at a glance, with nothing left over. In the sutras of the three baskets and twelve divisions there is no place you doubt and do not understand, no place you cannot explain; you know them all, with nothing remaining.
“In effortless cultivation, observing the mind is the most essential.”

Effortless cultivation” is cultivation without effort. To use the mind to cultivate the mind is cultivation with effort — having a mind that cultivates, using the mind to cultivate. Cultivation with effort is the preliminary stage, gradually passing over into cultivation without effort, that is, “effortless cultivation.” In effortless cultivation, “observing the mind is the most essential” — observing the mind is the most important. We said above that observing the mind is alertly watching where thoughts arise. When a thought comes, ask where it comes from; when the thought ceases, ask where it goes. Observing the mind is illuminating: observing it, shining upon it; thus thoughts will not arise and cease chaotically and flow on without cease. Without illumination, delusive thoughts fly about and ten thousand considerations arise, and you instead grow used to it and do not feel the confusion — how can that do? So one must be alert and watch it well. True mind and deluded mind, you must be clear about them. The mind that illuminates is still the deluded mind, because this too is raising the mind and stirring thoughts. Without the true mind, this deluded mind would not arise; the deluded mind is produced by the true mind, it is the true mind’s wondrous function. At the very time of using it, at the very time of observing the mind, do not discriminate whether it is true mind or deluded mind. When the use reaches the point where the deluded mind does not move, the mind that observes and the thought observed drop away at once — then “subject and object both perish,” and the observing mind and the observed thought are both gone. Without illumination one will not reach the perishing of subject and object, will not break open; therefore one must illuminate. Buddha-recitation is also illumination, also stopping and insight: “Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha…” The practitioner’s thoughts are gathered in by the Buddha-name, and the thoughts do not move — this is stopping. One recites oneself and hears oneself, hearing with utter distinctness — this is insight. Even without sound, reciting Amitābha in the mind, one hears it perfectly clearly — this is illumination. To attend to the Buddha-name and not let the mind stray is stopping; to illuminate the Buddha-name, clear and distinct, is insight. Observing the mind is not observing the lump of flesh that is the heart, but observing mental thoughts. In cultivating the Heart Center Dharma we too observe the mind. On the cushion we hold the mantra, mind reciting and ear hearing, reciting each word clearly and hearing with utter distinctness. Off the cushion we illuminate, alert to where thoughts arise, like a cat catching a mouse. The moment a thought arises we see it, do not turn with the thought, are not moved by states. To know as soon as a thought arises is what the Chan school calls “recognizing it” — recognizing it, and it is no injustice!

Someone says: when I do not recite the Buddha-name I am fine and have no deluded thoughts; as soon as I recite, it is ruined — deluded thoughts are beyond counting. Has Buddha-recitation ruined you? No! In fact when you were not reciting, your mind was terribly confused; you simply did not notice! You ran after deluded thoughts and after states, turning in the six paths of transmigration all along. Now that you recite the Buddha-name, the mind has quieted, and you see the deluded thoughts and see the cause of transmigration — this is a great good thing! It is like a room with a small hole: a beam of sunlight comes in, and you see the dust flying in that beam of light. Where there is no light, you cannot see the dust. In fact dust is everywhere; once the sunlight shines on it, it appears. So to see the thoughts is a good thing; this is the first revealing of the light of wisdom. You hope to have no thoughts at all at once — that is like hoping to ascend to heaven in one step; how could it be so quick? This is a common failing of students: everyone wants to succeed at once, to become a Buddha at once, and it is not so easy. Yet it is not hard either: once you know the method, go and do it — practice today, tomorrow, the day after — and in a few years you will certainly succeed. To want to succeed at once, in a single day, is not how it is. In cultivating the Heart Center Dharma, some sit for two hours a day and still feel miserable; after forcing themselves to sit a few days they cannot continue — this is ruinous for lack of perseverance. So they switch to scattered Buddha-recitation: the mouth says “Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha…” while the mind is awhirl with delusive thoughts — will that do? That is the same as not reciting the Buddha-name at all — it will not do!
“Only by transcending all extreme views, clingings, and pervasive imagining is there the true king of views.” (View)

Everyone has extreme views. What is an extreme view? Clinging to existence and clinging to nonexistence — this is the extreme of existence and nonexistence; clinging to good and clinging to bad — this is the extreme of good and bad. There are also long and short, right and wrong, gain and loss, empty and existent, and many other kinds of extreme views. Whatever is relative has two sides, and all are extreme views. Extreme views are the relative views of ordinary beings. What is clinging? To fix on a matter and be unable to let it go, unable to break free — that is clinging. What is pervasive imagining? To calculate and scheme universally, unable to let go of a single thing, wanting everything. This is what the Dharma-character school calls “the nature of pervasive imagining and clinging.” Every ordinary being in the six paths of transmigration is like this; there is not one ordinary being who does not calculate. Some say with their mouths that they do not want this and do not want that — do not believe them; in fact they want everything. “Fish is what I desire; bear’s paw is also what I desire” — they want both fish and bear’s paw. If they say there is one thing they do not want, it is only because they know they cannot have both. In fact none of it is obtainable! Alas, all is pervasive calculating! We practitioners must put all these things down, put everything down — not putting them down will not do! To put down is to transcend: “only by transcending all extreme views, clingings, and pervasive imagining is there the true king of views.” Only by doing so is there right knowledge and view, is there the king of views. Why? Because only by doing so does one accord with our original nature. “View” means to recognize our original nature, to recognize our original face. If you do not “view” in this way, how can you recognize the original nature? One must put down, depart from, and transcend all extreme views, clingings, and pervasive imagining — then there is the true king of views.
“In cultivation, one must be utterly unscattered from the luminous essence of one’s own mind; only then is there the true king of cultivation.” (Cultivation)

View, meditation, and action: what we have just discussed is “view”; now we discuss “meditation.” Meditation is “cultivation”: “one must be utterly unscattered from the luminous essence of one’s own mind; only then is there the true king of cultivation.” The luminous essence of one’s own mind is our own original nature; it is immeasurably luminous and infinitely wise, and so it is called the luminous essence — the light is on our own essence. One must not be scattered in the least, must not in the least be lured by outer states into leaving the essence of the self-nature. If one runs after states and thinks wildly, then one is scattered. One must at every moment see the original nature truly and clearly and be able to keep it. Only thus is there the true king of cultivation. We are all accustomed to running after states, and only after running ten thousand li do we realize: Oh! How far I have run after deluded thoughts — pull it back! But by then it feels too late. There is a saying in the Chan school: “Do not fear the arising of a thought; fear only that awareness is late.” It tells us to be vigilant and illumine at every moment, not to turn with deluded thoughts. If you have run far and long after deluded thoughts before you know it, that is not good. Let thoughts arise as they will, but the moment one arises I can see it. The moment I see it and pay it no attention, it is illuminated through. To illuminate through is to be utterly unscattered; only this is the true king of cultivation.
“In action, one must abide peacefully in the luminous essence of one’s own mind, without doing and without seeking; only then is there the true king of action.” (Action)

Action is practice. How does one practice? “One must abide peacefully in the luminous essence of one’s own mind, without doing and without seeking; only then is there the true king of action.” Here the luminous essence of one’s own mind is mentioned once more. One must abide peacefully on this immeasurably luminous, infinitely wise essence, “without doing and without seeking.” Without doing means not deliberately fabricating; accord with conditions and be spontaneous in all things. Some people, when cultivating, do not cultivate according to the Dharma but always add something clever of their own — this is deliberate fabrication. Without seeking means seeking nothing at all. Do not seek superknowledges, do not seek to enter concentration. The more you seek concentration, the less you can enter it; the more you seek superknowledges, the less they appear. Because you have raised deluded thoughts and obscured the mind’s light. One must be “without doing and without seeking” — only thus is there “the true king of action.” If one does not cultivate in this way, then even with diligent cultivation one cannot accomplish the Way; because you do not know what the luminous essence of your own mind is, it is like cooking rice with sand — in the end it cannot be accomplished. First one must know what the luminous essence of one’s own mind is, and then protect this luminous essence of one’s own mind. Whether reciting the Buddha-name, holding mantras, or illuminating, the aim of all is to protect this luminous essence of one’s own mind. This is the prerequisite, and it is extremely important. Applying effort thus, one will certainly succeed, and so it is called “the king of action.” If one does not know what the luminous essence of one’s own mind is, then all is blind practice and wild striving, always circling outside and never reaching the center; in the end one cannot accomplish the Way.

“If one speaks of the way of the fruit, one must have no seeking and no abiding regarding sage and ordinary being, high and low, nirvāṇa, and birth-and-death; only the truly unsurpassed ‘accord with conditions yet unchanging, unchanging yet according with conditions,’ still yet ever illumining, illumining yet ever still, equal to all Buddhas — this is the fruit.” (Fruit)

The Ganges Great Mudrā has always stressed the three essentials of “view, meditation, and action.” Why? In order to realize the holy fruit. View, meditation, and action are only the means; realizing the holy fruit is the goal. “If one speaks of the way of the fruit”: if one were to say what counts as realizing the holy fruit, “one must have no seeking regarding sage and ordinary being, high and low, nirvāṇa, and birth-and-death.” Sage or ordinary, high or low, nirvāṇa or birth-and-death — these are all distinctions of our deluded mind. We are originally Buddhas, originally never apart from the great Way. Our essence is neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; “mind, Buddha, and sentient beings” are three without difference — what sage and ordinary, what high and low, what birth-and-death and nirvāṇa is there? In the ultimate there are no such relativities; what would you still seek? When one truly realizes the essence, there is no sage and no ordinary; sages and ordinary beings are one body, all the original luminous self-nature. Since there is no sage and no ordinary, what high and low is there? There is no “I am above, you are below,” no “you are above, I am below”; there is no pride or arrogance, and all are equal and one suchness — high and low are fundamentally unobtainable. Nirvāṇa yet unborn, nirvāṇa yet undestroyed: the essence was never born or extinguished to begin with — what nirvāṇa can be spoken of? Since there is no nirvāṇa, what birth-and-death is there? So it is said that there was fundamentally no birth-and-death, and to speak further of ending birth and escaping death is quite superfluous! Since everything is fundamentally nonexistent, what is there to seek? Therefore it is said, “have no seeking at all.”

No abiding”: the true nirvāṇa is “the nirvāṇa of no abiding place.” We said before that there are four kinds of nirvāṇa. First, the nirvāṇa of self-nature. The self-nature is our true mind; it is fundamentally unborn and undestroyed, fundamentally nirvāṇa. Second, nirvāṇa with remainder. This is what Hīnayāna sages realize; transformation birth-and-death is not yet ended, and so it is called “with remainder.” Third, nirvāṇa without remainder. Transformation birth-and-death too is ended, and everything is gone. This is the nirvāṇa realized by the Buddha in the Hīnayāna teachings. Fourth, the nirvāṇa of no abiding place. Even Buddhahood is unobtainable; this alone is true nirvāṇa, the saying “birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are alike flowers in the sky.” At this point anything at all can exist, anywhere at all can be dwelt in: nothing is not possessed, nowhere is not present. “Formerly the true was all false; now the false is all true. One only restores the original nature — not one dharma is new.” No abiding, not even abiding in nirvāṇa — then one can abide anywhere. We asked above: after parinirvāṇa, into what place is one born? The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Eastern Pure Lapis Lazuli World, or the Inner Court of Tuṣita? “One should abide in nothing”; to abide in something is wrong. The Buddha is fundamentally markless, accords with all conditions, constantly accords with beings, tumbles along with beings; wherever there is a karmic connection, there one goes to save beings, with no fixed place. Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha is not born in a pure land but saves beings in hell: “So long as hell is not empty, I vow not to become a Buddha.” Do you think Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha has not become a Buddha? Do you think Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha is not in a pure land? In fact hell was originally empty; Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha became a Buddha long ago, and at every moment and in every place he is within the pure land. In the eyes of beings it is hell, because beings have a hellish mind (a mind in which greed, anger, and delusion blaze). Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha has no hellish mind; for him every place is a pure land.

No abiding” is “the truly unsurpassed accord with conditions yet unchanging, unchanging yet according with conditions.” To accord with conditions yet be unchanging is to accord with the conditions of all beings. If beings are in heaven, I go to heaven; if beings are in hell, I go to hell. Ascending to heaven or entering the earth, the original nature does not change. Ascending to heaven, it is not increased by a fraction or made purer by a fraction; descending to earth, it is not decreased by a fraction or made more defiled by a fraction. Take gold: according to conditions it is beaten into a ring, into a necklace, into a bracelet; according to conditions it takes different forms, but the essence of the gold does not change, and the gold is still gold. Unchanging yet according with conditions: though the essence of the gold does not change, its forms can change — this is precisely wondrous function, and the true mind is complete in boundless wondrous function. According with conditions yet unchanging is the essence; unchanging yet according with conditions is the wondrous function. “Still yet ever illumining, illumining yet ever still”: still means still and unmoving — the essence is still and unmoving; illumining means illumining the ten thousand dharmas — to be able to illumine the ten thousand dharmas is wondrous function. This too speaks of essence and wondrous function. We spoke above of enlightened illumination: one must be aware and alert at every moment, not run after states. At the later stage even awareness is no longer needed; if there is still awareness present, there is still doing. Only without doing can it be called “non-doing.” When the practice is mature, one need not raise enlightened illumination; it illumines of itself. Not raising enlightened illumination is stillness; illumining of itself is illumination. This is “still yet ever illumining.” And “illumining yet ever still”? However much wondrous function arises, the essence remains suchness, unmoving. Only when the practice has reached this point is one at home; if there is still enlightened illumination present, one is not yet home. But one cannot reach this all at once; one must always pass through the stage of raising enlightened illumination. One must illumine, illumine, and illumine again, until one is thoroughly familiar with it — like a person in the air who forgets that there is air. “As one who enters a room of orchids, after long smelling it no longer perceives the fragrance”: one is wholly transformed and oblivious.

To be like all Buddhas, “according with conditions yet unchanging, unchanging yet according with conditions”; to be like all Buddhas, “still yet ever illumining, illumining yet ever still” — this is to be equal to all Buddhas. “Equal to all Buddhas — this is the fruit”: only thus does one count as having realized the fruit. When we first begin to apply effort, we must know what the original nature is. Having known the original nature, we must often observe the mind and often illumine. Practicing thus, one can realize the fruit of Buddhahood. If one does not illumine and does not practice, how can one realize the fruit? To ascend to heaven in one step is impossible; there is no one born a Buddha. Because his ignorance is still there, he always clings to marks. As soon as an infant has awareness it knows the body matters, and it too is full of selfishness. If it has something, it will not give it to you; if you take its things, it cries and makes a fuss. This is all because of ignorance! Therefore, to realize the fruit of the Way one must begin by opening right knowledge and view. The first step: “pa —” the original is opened, ah! This is my self-nature! The second step: at every moment and in every place apply effort to protect it. The third step is realizing the fruit. If you can truly recognize the self-nature today and then recite the Buddha-name, you will certainly obtain great enjoyment. Then Buddha-recitation is different from before. Before, reciting the Buddha-name you did not know what “reciting” was; you only knew to seek toward the West. Now you understand: Oh! These phrases of the Buddha-name are reciting my self-nature and making my own mind pure. “Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha…” sweeping away all the defilement of your own mind, cutting off the clinging and afflictions of your own mind at the root — then Buddha-recitation brings you true enjoyment. Therefore opening right knowledge and view is extremely important; “view” comes first. When “view” is right, one can attain right meditation, and only then is cultivation right action.
